claim: PIEZO channels transmit mechanical force signals to cells, allowing them to make critical decisions during development and in pathophysiological conditions.
source: PIEZO channels transmit mechanical force signals to cells, allowing them to make critical decisions during development and in pathophysiological conditions.
evidence: This is a general statement about PIEZO channel function that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: hPIEZO1 has a more flattened and extended architecture than curved mouse PIEZO1 (mPIEZO1).
source: Our results suggest that hPIEZO1 has a more flattened and extended architecture than curved mouse PIEZO1 (mPIEZO1).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data presented in the manuscript, including cryo-EM structures and measurements.

claim: Multi-lipidated MDFIC subunits insert laterally into the hPIEZO1 pore module like mPIEZO1.
source: The multi-lipidated MDFIC subunits insert laterally into the hPIEZO1 pore module like mPIEZO1, resulting in a more curved and extended state.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data showing the position of MDFIC in the hPIEZO1 structure.

claim: MDFIC binding results in a more curved and extended state of hPIEZO1.
source: The multi-lipidated MDFIC subunits insert laterally into the hPIEZO1 pore module like mPIEZO1, resulting in a more curved and extended state.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison data between hPIEZO1 with and without MDFIC.

claim: Pore lipids directly seal the central hydrophobic pore of hPIEZO1.
source: Interestingly, the high-resolution structures suggest that the pore lipids, which directly seal the central hydrophobic pore, may be involved in the rapid inactivation of hPIEZO1.
evidence: This is supported by high-resolution cryo-EM density maps showing lipid density in the pore region.

claim: Pore lipids may be involved in the rapid inactivation of hPIEZO1.
source: Interestingly, the high-resolution structures suggest that the pore lipids, which directly seal the central hydrophobic pore, may be involved in the rapid inactivation of hPIEZO1.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on structural observations and inference from the data.

claim: The R2456H mutation significantly slows down the inactivation of hPIEZO1.
source: While the severe hereditary erythrocytosis mutant R2456H significantly slows down the inactivation of hPIEZO1, the hPIEZO1-R2456H-MDFIC complex shows a more curved and contracted structure with an inner helix twist due to the broken link between the pore lipid and R2456H.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing inactivation kinetics.

claim: The hPIEZO1-R2456H-MDFIC complex shows a more curved and contracted structure with an inner helix twist.
source: While the severe hereditary erythrocytosis mutant R2456H significantly slows down the inactivation of hPIEZO1, the hPIEZO1-R2456H-MDFIC complex shows a more curved and contracted structure with an inner helix twist due to the broken link between the pore lipid and R2456H.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data of the R2456H mutant complex.

claim: The structural changes in hPIEZO1-R2456H-MDFIC are due to the broken link between the pore lipid and R2456H.
source: While the severe hereditary erythrocytosis mutant R2456H significantly slows down the inactivation of hPIEZO1, the hPIEZO1-R2456H-MDFIC complex shows a more curved and contracted structure with an inner helix twist due to the broken link between the pore lipid and R2456H.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison and the position of the mutation.

claim: In bacteria, MscS and large-conductance mechanosensitive channel are responsible for bacterial force sensing.
source: In bacteria, two major MS channels, the small-conductance mechanosensitive channel (MscS) (Levina et al., 1999) and large-conductance mechanosensitive channel (Sukharev et al., 1994), are responsible for bacterial force sensing.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In mammals, PIEZO, K2P, and TMEM63 channels have been identified as bona fide MS channels.
source: In contrast, in mammals, only the PIEZO (Coste et al., 2010), two-pore domain K+ channel (K2P) (Maingret et al., 1999) and TMEM63 (Murthy et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018), channels have been identified as bona fide MS channels.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Human PIEZO1 exhibits faster inactivation gating kinetics than mouse PIEZO1 under the same voltage condition.
source: Human PIEZO1 (hPIEZO1) exhibits faster inactivation gating kinetics than mouse PIEZO1 (mPIEZO1) under the same voltage condition (Coste et al., 2010; Zheng et al., 2019; Bae et al., 2013), so mPIEZO1 presents a native gain-of-function ('GOF') state relative to hPIEZO1 regarding inactivation gating kinetics.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: mPIEZO1 presents a native gain-of-function state relative to hPIEZO1 regarding inactivation gating kinetics.
source: Human PIEZO1 (hPIEZO1) exhibits faster inactivation gating kinetics than mouse PIEZO1 (mPIEZO1) under the same voltage condition (Coste et al., 2010; Zheng et al., 2019; Bae et al., 2013), so mPIEZO1 presents a native gain-of-function ('GOF') state relative to hPIEZO1 regarding inactivation gating kinetics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of inactivation kinetics between species.

claim: MDFIC/MDFI is an auxiliary subunit of PIEZO channels that prolongs inactivation and reduces mechanosensitivity.
source: Also, it has been reported recently that the MyoD family inhibitor, MDFIC/MDFI, is an auxiliary subunit of PIEZO channels to prolong inactivation and reduce mechanosensitivity (Zhou et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Some hereditary erythrocytosis mutations exhibit slower inactivation gating kinetics than wild-type hPIEZO1.
source: Besides, some hereditary erythrocytosis (HX) mutations exhibit slower inactivation gating kinetics than wild-type hPIEZO1.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data and citations.

claim: Slower inactivation in HX mutations may result in higher open probability and delayed inactivation of hPIEZO1.
source: The slower inactivation may result in the higher open probability and delayed inactivation of hPIEZO1; thus, these mutations are considered GOF (Bae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between inactivation kinetics and channel function.

claim: HX mutations are considered gain-of-function mutations.
source: The slower inactivation may result in the higher open probability and delayed inactivation of hPIEZO1; thus, these mutations are considered GOF (Bae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation and inference from functional data.

claim: HX is an autosomal dominant disorder that causes dehydration of red blood cells, resulting in hemolytic anemia.
source: HX, also known as inherited dehydrated stomatocytosis, is an autosomal dominant disorder that causes dehydration of red blood cells, resulting in hemolytic anemia.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about the disease.

claim: Some HX mutations show alterations in response to osmotic pressure and in membrane protein trafficking.
source: In addition to changes in gating kinetics, some of the HX mutations show alterations in response to osmotic pressure and in membrane protein trafficking (Glogowska et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Populations with a mild GOF PIEZO1 allele are likely to be resistant to malaria infection.
source: Interestingly, the populations with a mild GOF PIEZO1 allele are likely to be resistant to malaria infection, while some present a strong association with increased plasma iron (Ma et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to population genetics studies.

claim: Some populations with mild GOF PIEZO1 alleles present a strong association with increased plasma iron.
source: Interestingly, the populations with a mild GOF PIEZO1 allele are likely to be resistant to malaria infection, while some present a strong association with increased plasma iron (Ma et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to population genetics studies.

claim: The codon-optimized full-length hPIEZO1 construct exhibits similar mechanosensitivity and fast inactivation gating properties as previously reported.
source: To resolve this, we synthesized a codon-optimized full-length hPIEZO1 with a C-terminal GFP and flag tag into the pBM vector (Goehring et al., 2014), and this construct exhibits similar mechanosensitivity and fast inactivation gating properties as previously reported by whole-cell poking assay (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figures.

claim: The smeared bands around 300 kDa on SDS-PAGE indicate the potential presence of posttranslational modifications.
source: The smeared bands around 300 kDa on SDS-PAGE indicate the potential presence of posttranslational modifications (PTMs), and the lower bands may be the binding partners or degraded fragments of hPIEZO1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a and b).
evidence: This is an inference based on the appearance of protein bands on SDS-PAGE.

claim: The lower bands on SDS-PAGE may be the binding partners or degraded fragments of hPIEZO1.
source: The smeared bands around 300 kDa on SDS-PAGE indicate the potential presence of posttranslational modifications (PTMs), and the lower bands may be the binding partners or degraded fragments of hPIEZO1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a and b).
evidence: This is speculation based on the appearance of protein bands on SDS-PAGE.

claim: A cryo-EM density map of hPIEZO1 was obtained at a total resolution of 3.3 Å from approximately 87K particles.
source: The purified hPIEZO1 protein was subjected to the standard cryo-EM workflow, resulting in a cryo-EM density map at a total resolution of 3.3 Å from approximately 87K particles (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a–e) that allowed us to build a near-atomic model of hPIEZO1 (Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is directly supported by the cryo-EM data collection and processing.

claim: Among the nine transmembrane helix units predicted by primary sequences, the two N-terminal ones are not visible in the cryo-EM density map.
source: Among the nine transmembrane helix units (THUs) containing four transmembrane helices for each predicted by primary sequences, the two N-terminal ones are not visible in the cryo-EM density map.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density map.

claim: The hPIEZO1 density map shows a disk approximately 30 nm wide.
source: The hPIEZO1 density map, filtered with a low-pass filter, shows a disk approximately 30 nm wide with a horn-like density in the peripheral blade region, likely due to the PTMs such as glycosylation.
evidence: This is a measurement from the cryo-EM density map.

claim: The horn-like density in the peripheral blade region is likely due to PTMs such as glycosylation.
source: The hPIEZO1 density map, filtered with a low-pass filter, shows a disk approximately 30 nm wide with a horn-like density in the peripheral blade region, likely due to the PTMs such as glycosylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the appearance and location of the density.

claim: A large density below the central pore module at the intracellular side may be potential auxiliary subunits.
source: Interestingly, we see a large density below the central pore module at the intracellular side, which may be potential auxiliary subunits, consistent with the lower molecular weight bands on SDS-PAGE (Figure 1b–g, Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is speculation based on the cryo-EM density and SDS-PAGE results.

claim: The blades of hPIEZO1 are about 5 Å down toward the cytoplasmic side compared to mPIEZO1.
source: Structural comparison of hPIEZO1 and curved mPIEZO1 shows that hPIEZO1 presents a more flattened structure from the side view (Figure 2a). The blades of hPIEZO1 are about 5 Å down toward the cytoplasmic side than those of mPIEZO1.
evidence: This is a measurement from structural comparison.

claim: The cap domain of hPIEZO1 is slightly upward to the extracellular side compared to mPIEZO1.
source: Meanwhile, the cap domain of hPIEZO1 is slightly upward to the extracellular side (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is an observation from structural comparison.

claim: The distal blades of hPIEZO1 rotate counterclockwise about 22 Å compared to mPIEZO1.
source: In the top view, the distal blades rotate counterclockwise about 22 Å compared to mPIEZO1 (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a measurement from structural comparison.

claim: hPIEZO1 appears more extended than the curved mPIEZO1.
source: Therefore, hPIEZO1 appears more extended than the curved mPIEZO1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural measurements.

claim: hPIEZO1 still maintains a sizeable curved state compared to the flattened mPIEZO1 structure.
source: Meanwhile, hPIEZO1 still maintains a sizeable curved state compared to the flattened mPIEZO1 structure.
evidence: This is an observation from structural comparison.

claim: The pore radius of hPIEZO1 is between that of the curved and flattened mPIEZO1.
source: The pore radius of hPIEZO1 is between that of the curved and flattened mPIEZO1.
evidence: This is a measurement from structural analysis.

claim: The curved hPIEZO1 may still represent a nonconducting state.
source: Therefore, the curved hPIEZO1 may still represent a nonconducting state (Figure 2e–h), and the differences in curvature and pore radius may be implicated in channel gating properties of hPIEZO1 and mPIEZO1.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural features and pore radius measurements.

claim: The differences in curvature and pore radius may be implicated in channel gating properties of hPIEZO1 and mPIEZO1.
source: Therefore, the curved hPIEZO1 may still represent a nonconducting state (Figure 2e–h), and the differences in curvature and pore radius may be implicated in channel gating properties of hPIEZO1 and mPIEZO1.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural differences.

claim: The three hPIEZO1 channelopathy GOF mutants may be structurally less stable than wild type.
source: Based on these results, these three hPIEZO1 channelopathy GOF mutants may be structurally less stable than wild type.
evidence: This is an inference based on the difficulty in obtaining high-resolution structures of the mutants.

claim: A 3.7 Å resolution cryo-EM density map was obtained for hPIEZO1-A1988V.
source: We then tried and obtained almost twice as many hPIEZO1-A1988V images as the wild type but only achieved a 3.7 Å resolution cryo-EM density map (Table 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly stated from the cryo-EM data collection.

claim: The overall structure of hPIEZO1-A1988V is similar to the wild type.
source: Yet, the resulting overall structure is similar to the wild type (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from structural comparison.

claim: A 3.0 Å resolution cryo-EM density map was obtained for the hPIEZO1-MDFIC complex.
source: We obtained a 3.0 Å resolution cryo-EM density map of the hPIEZO1-MDFIC complex (Table 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly stated from the cryo-EM data collection.

claim: MDFIC induces a more curved and contracted architecture in hPIEZO1 from the side and top views.
source: Interestingly, while MDFIC does not significantly alter the curvature of mPIEZO1, it induces a more curved and contracted architecture in hPIEZO1 from the side and top views, respectively (Figure 3g and h).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: MDFIC does not significantly alter the curvature of mPIEZO1.
source: Interestingly, while MDFIC does not significantly alter the curvature of mPIEZO1, it induces a more curved and contracted architecture in hPIEZO1 from the side and top views, respectively (Figure 3g and h).
evidence: This is an observation from comparison with previous mPIEZO1 structures.

claim: MDFIC decelerates hPIEZO1 inactivation and weakens its mechanosensitivity by remodeling the pore module and exerting more blade curvature.
source: Combining with the similar effect of MDFIC on mPIEZO1 (Zhou et al., 2023) and hPIEZO1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we suspect that MDFIC decelerates hPIEZO1 inactivation and weakens its mechanosensitivity by remodeling the pore module and exerting more blade curvature.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and functional data.

claim: Co-expression of channelopathy mutants with MDFIC resulted in significantly reduced mechanosensitivity and inactivation rate.
source: Indeed, electrophysiological studies showed that co-expression of these channelopathy mutants with MDFIC resulted in significantly reduced mechanosensitivity and inactivation rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data.

claim: MDFIC stabilizes the GOF channelopathy mutants structurally.
source: These results further suggest that MDFIC stabilizes the GOF channelopathy mutants structurally.
evidence: This is an inference based on the improved quality of cryo-EM data for mutants co-expressed with MDFIC.

claim: Cryo-EM density maps were obtained for hPIEZO1-A1988V-MDFIC and hPIEZO1-E756del-MDFIC with overall resolutions of 3.1 and 2.8 Å, respectively.
source: Cryo-EM density maps were obtained for hPIEZO1-A1988V-MDFIC and hPIEZO1-E756del-MDFIC with overall resolutions of 3.1 and 2.8 Å, respectively (Table 1, Figure 4—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This is directly stated from the cryo-EM data collection.

claim: The resolution of hPIEZO1-R2456H-MDFIC was improved to 4.6 Å with 16K particles.
source: The resolution of hPIEZO1-R2456H-MDFIC was improved to 4.6 Å with 16K particles, allowing us to build a relatively accurate model of the transmembrane helices based on the hPIEZO1-MDFIC model (Table 1, Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is directly stated from the cryo-EM data collection.

claim: The hPIEZO1-R2456H-MDFIC shows a smaller disk of 25 nm compared to the 30 nm for the wild type and the other two mutants.
source: On the other hand, the hPIEZO1-R2456H-MDFIC shows a smaller disk of 25 nm compared to the 30 nm for the wild type and the other two mutants (Figure 5a–f).
evidence: This is a measurement from the cryo-EM density map.

claim: The smaller disk of hPIEZO1-R2456H-MDFIC is mainly due to the more significant contraction of the blade arms and a more curved state compared to the wild-type hPIEZO1-MDFIC.
source: The smaller disk is mainly due to the more significant contraction of the blade arms and a more curved state compared to the wild-type hPIEZO1-MDFIC in the side view (Figure 5g and h).
evidence: This is an observation from structural comparison.

claim: The IH of hPIEZO1-R2456H-MDFIC showed a significant twist of ~35° compared to wild-type hPIEZO1-MDFIC.
source: Surprisingly, the IH of hPIEZO1-R2456H-MDFIC showed a significant twist of ~35° compared to wild-type hPIEZO1-MDFIC (Figure 6g and h).
evidence: This is a measurement from structural comparison.

claim: The coiled-coil shape of the IH pore in hPIEZO1-R2456H-MDFIC results in a more dilated pore on the extracellular side.
source: The coiled-coil shape of the IH pore results in a more dilated pore on the extracellular side (Figure 5i–l), suggesting that unlike the mild GOF E756del and A1988V mutations present in the typical African population and located in the THUs region, the more severe mutation R2456H, which is located in the IH, not only leads to blade reshaping but also results in pore expansion (Figure 6d–h).
evidence: This is an observation from structural analysis.

claim: The R2456H mutation, located in the IH, not only leads to blade reshaping but also results in pore expansion.
source: The coiled-coil shape of the IH pore results in a more dilated pore on the extracellular side (Figure 5i–l), suggesting that unlike the mild GOF E756del and A1988V mutations present in the typical African population and located in the THUs region, the more severe mutation R2456H, which is located in the IH, not only leads to blade reshaping but also results in pore expansion (Figure 6d–h).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison.

claim: An apparent lipid density was found in wild-type hPIEZO1-MDFIC, hPIEZO1-A1988V-MDFIC, and hPIEZO1-E756del-MDFIC in the pore module.
source: We were surprised to find an apparent lipid density in wild-type hPIEZO1-MDFIC, hPIEZO1-A1988V-MDFIC, and even more evident in the 2.8 Å resolution map of hPIEZO1-E756del-MDFIC in the pore module, where one of its hydrophobic fatty acid tails inserts into the hydrophobic pore formed by I2447, V2450, and F2454, thus sealing the pore to prevent ion flow (Figure 6a–c).
evidence: This is an observation from high-resolution cryo-EM density maps.

claim: One hydrophobic fatty acid tail of the pore lipid inserts into the hydrophobic pore formed by I2447, V2450, and F2454, thus sealing the pore to prevent ion flow.
source: We were surprised to find an apparent lipid density in wild-type hPIEZO1-MDFIC, hPIEZO1-A1988V-MDFIC, and even more evident in the 2.8 Å resolution map of hPIEZO1-E756del-MDFIC in the pore module, where one of its hydrophobic fatty acid tails inserts into the hydrophobic pore formed by I2447, V2450, and F2454, thus sealing the pore to prevent ion flow (Figure 6a–c).
evidence: This is an observation and interpretation from the cryo-EM density map.

claim: The hydrophilic phosphate head of the pore lipid interacts directly with R2456 on the side of the IH of the pore.
source: Even more surprisingly, the hydrophilic phosphate head interacts directly with R2456, a residue with the more severe form of GOF mutation, on the side of the IH of the pore.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density map.

claim: Another fatty acid chain of the pore lipid interacts with the acyl chains of the covalently linked MDFIC lipids, forming a stable hPIEZO1-multi-lipidated MDFIC-pore lipid complex.
source: In addition, another fatty acid chain of the pore lipid interacts with the acyl chains of the covalently linked MDFIC lipids, forming a stable hPIEZO1-multi-lipidated MDFIC-pore lipid complex (Figure 6a–c).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density map.

claim: In wild-type hPIEZO1, similar pore lipids insert into the hydrophobic pore interacting with R2456.
source: We also carefully checked the corresponding pore lipid configuration in the 3.3 Å resolution map of hPIEZO1 and the 3.8 Å resolution map of hPIEZO1-A1988V without the multi-lipidated MDFIC auxiliary subunit and found that in wild-type hPIEZO1, similar pore lipids also insert into the hydrophobic pore interacting with R2456 (Figure 7a and f).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density map.

claim: In the mild GOF hPIEZO1-A1988V, the acyl chains of the pore lipid are retracted from the central hydrophobic pore to the side of the IH, although the hydrophilic phosphate group heads still interact with R2456.
source: However, in the mild GOF hPIEZO1-A1988V, which has a slower inactivation rate compared to wild-type hPIEZO1, the acyl chains of the pore lipid are retracted from the central hydrophobic pore to the side of the IH, although the hydrophilic phosphate group heads still interact with R2456 (Figure 7b and f).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density map.

claim: R2456 plays a critical role in anchoring lipids at the pore module.
source: These results reveal a critical role of R2456 in anchoring lipids at the pore module.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations of lipid-R2456 interactions.

claim: Substitution of the hydrophobic pore formed by I2447, V2450, and F2454 with a hydrophilic pore prolongs the inactivation time for both PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 channels.
source: The evidence supporting this model is based on previous electrophysiological functional studies that substitution of the hydrophobic pore, formed by I2447, V2450, and F2454, with a hydrophilic pore prolongs the inactivation time for both PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 channels (Zheng et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous functional studies.

claim: In the HX channelopathy mutant R2456H, the interaction between the hydrophilic phosphate group head and R2456 is disrupted, which leads to remodeling of the blade and pore module.
source: More robust evidence comes from the HX channelopathy mutant R2456H, wherein the interaction between the hydrophilic phosphate group head and R2456 is disrupted, which leads to remodeling of the blade and pore module (Figure 6d–h), thus significantly prolonging the inactivation time.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and functional data.

claim: In curved and flattened mPIEZO1 structures, pore lipids are occupying the similar lateral side of the pore, but not sealing the pore like the hPIEZO1-A1988V mutant.
source: Consistently, in curved and flattened mPIEZO1 structures (Yang et al., 2022), pore lipids are occupying the similar lateral side of the pore, but not sealing the pore like the hPIEZO1-A1988V mutant (Figures 7d–e–8c).
evidence: This is an observation from comparison with published mPIEZO1 structures.

claim: The curved and flattened mPIEZO1 structures are not sealed by pore lipid and thus may not adopt the deep inactivation state.
source: Similarly, we suspect that the curved and flattened mPIEZO1 structures are not sealed by pore lipid and thus may not adopt the deep inactivation state, consistent with electrophysiological results showing a slower inactivation manner of mPIEZO1 (Coste et al., 2010; Bae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculation based on structural observations and cited electrophysiological data.

claim: The multi-lipidated MDFIC functions to stabilize the pore lipids that seal the hydrophobic pore through interactions between hydrophobic acyl chain tails of the pore lipids and the lipids covalently linked to MDFIC.
source: The multi-lipidated MDFIC functions to stabilize the pore lipids that seal the hydrophobic pore further through interactions between hydrophobic acyl chain tails of the pore lipids and the lipids covalently linked to MDFIC (Figure 7c and f).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: Once activated, the PIEZO-MDFIC complexes assume much slower inactivation.
source: Once activated, the PIEZO-MDFIC complexes assume much slower inactivation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with the model that the multi-lipidated MDFIC makes the PIEZO challenging to open by mechanical force (Figure 8b and d).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data.

claim: The multi-lipidated MDFIC makes the PIEZO challenging to open by mechanical force.
source: Once activated, the PIEZO-MDFIC complexes assume much slower inactivation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with the model that the multi-lipidated MDFIC makes the PIEZO challenging to open by mechanical force (Figure 8b and d).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and functional data.

claim: The hPIEZO1-MDFIC/hPIEZO1-A1988V-MDFIC/hPIEZO1-E756del-MDFIC reshape the pore module and fall into a deep resting state.
source: Therefore, we deduce that the hPIEZO1-MDFIC/hPIEZO1-A1988V-MDFIC/hPIEZO1-E756del-MDFIC reshape the pore module and fall into a deep resting state, in which it becomes rather tricky to remove the pore lipid from the hydrophobic pore by mild mechanical force.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: In the deep resting state, it becomes rather tricky to remove the pore lipid from the hydrophobic pore by mild mechanical force.
source: Therefore, we deduce that the hPIEZO1-MDFIC/hPIEZO1-A1988V-MDFIC/hPIEZO1-E756del-MDFIC reshape the pore module and fall into a deep resting state, in which it becomes rather tricky to remove the pore lipid from the hydrophobic pore by mild mechanical force.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural model.

claim: Once the pore lipids are removed by a higher threshold of mechanical force, it is equally more difficult for the pore lipids to return to the hydrophobic pore region and regain the stable pore module-multi-lipidated MDFIC-pore lipid complex, thus resulting in the very prolonged slow inactivation phenotype.
source: On the other hand, once the pore lipids are removed by a higher threshold of the mechanical force, it is equally more difficult for the pore lipids to return to the hydrophobic pore region and regain the stable pore module-multi-lipidated MDFIC-pore lipid complex, thus resulting in the very prolonged slow inactivation phenotype (Figure 8b and d).
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural model and functional data.

claim: MyoD was the first transcription factor identified to specify cell fate in a cell-autonomous fashion.
source: MyoD was the first transcription factor identified to specify cell fate in a cell-autonomous fashion, ushering decades of investigation into cell fate control that led to the discovery of iPSC reprogramming (Chambers and Studer, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: MyoD interacting proteins MDFIC and MDFI are auxiliary factors for the PIEZO MS ion channels.
source: It is intriguing that MyoD interacting proteins MDFIC and MDFI are auxiliary factors for the PIEZO MS ion channels, suggesting that these complexes link cell force sensing and cell fate control (Zhou et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent research.

claim: PIEZO-MDFIC/MDFI complexes link cell force sensing and cell fate control.
source: It is intriguing that MyoD interacting proteins MDFIC and MDFI are auxiliary factors for the PIEZO MS ion channels, suggesting that these complexes link cell force sensing and cell fate control (Zhou et al., 2023).
evidence: This is speculation based on the functional roles of the proteins.

claim: Mice with PIEZO deletions are lethal.
source: Indeed, mice with PIEZO deletions are lethal, supporting the idea that mechanosensing through these channels is critical in cell fate control during development.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous research.

claim: Mechanosensing through PIEZO channels is critical in cell fate control during development.
source: Indeed, mice with PIEZO deletions are lethal, supporting the idea that mechanosensing through these channels is critical in cell fate control during development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lethality of PIEZO deletions.

claim: MDFIC enables hPIEZO1 to respond to different forces by modifying the pore module through lipid interactions.
source: MDFIC enables hPIEZO1 to respond to different forces by modifying the pore module through lipid interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural and functional data presented.

claim: The inactivation rate of PIEZO channels is essential for the physiological functions of different cell types, including neuronal and non-neuronal cells.
source: Mechanistically, inactivation follows different principles in different ion channels (Sukomon et al., 2023). The inactivation rate of PIEZO channels is essential for the physiological functions of different cell types, including neuronal and non-neuronal cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Different subtypes and species of PIEZO channels exhibit different inactivation rates.
source: Moreover, different subtypes and species of PIEZO channels exhibit different inactivation rates.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous research.

claim: hPIEZO1 and mPIEZO2 have a faster inactivation rate than mPIEZO1.
source: For example, hPIEZO1 and mPIEZO2 have a faster inactivation rate than mPIEZO1 (Coste et al., 2010; Anishkin et al., 2014; Bae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Abnormal inactivation of the PIEZO channel is one of the dominant outcomes of clinical PIEZO channelopathy.
source: More importantly, abnormal inactivation of the PIEZO channel is one of the dominant outcomes of clinical PIEZO channelopathy (Coste et al., 2010; Bae et al., 2013).
